subject: chem
title: Polymerisation
subtitle: Addition and condensation polymers, properties and disposal.
concept: Addition polymers form when alkene monomers undergo addition reactions across their C=C bonds; no small molecule is lost.
Condensation polymers form when difunctional monomers join with loss of a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each step.
Polymer properties depend on chain length, branching, cross-linking and the forces between chains; disposal is an environmental concern.

notes.heading: Addition Polymerisation
items: Addition polymers form when many alkene (or substituted alkene) monomers undergo addition across the C=C bond — no atoms are lost. The repeat unit has the same atomic composition as the monomer.

Low-density poly(ethene) (LDPE) is branched — chains cannot pack closely, giving lower density, flexibility, and a lower melting point. High-density poly(ethene) (HDPE, Ziegler–Natta catalyst) has linear chains that pack closely — higher density and melting point.
Addition polymers are chemically inert and non-biodegradable — disposal by landfill or incineration (PVC releases toxic HCl on burning) is problematic.

notes.heading: Condensation Polymerisation
items: Condensation polymers form from difunctional monomers that react together with the loss of a small molecule (usually water, sometimes HCl) at each step.
Polyesters (–COO– linkage): e.g. Terylene/PET from ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Polyamides (–CONH– linkage): e.g. nylon-6,6 from hexane-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid.
Condensation polymers can be hydrolysed under acidic or basic conditions — unlike addition polymers. This also means they are more biodegradable.

definitions.body: A polymer formed by repeated addition of alkene monomers across C=C double bonds; no small molecule is lost.
A polymer formed by condensation reactions between difunctional monomers, with elimination of a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each step.
A small molecule that can undergo polymerisation to form a polymer.

workedExamples.q: Draw a section of nylon-6,6 and identify the amide link.

steps.text: –NH₂ + HOOC– → –NH–CO– + H₂O. One amide bond formed per monomer unit.

mistakes: Drawing the repeat unit of an addition polymer without showing continuation brackets and subscript n.
Confusing the linkage in polyesters (–COO–) with polyamides (–CONH–).
Stating all polymers are non-biodegradable — condensation polymers CAN be hydrolysed; addition polymers cannot.
tips: To write a repeat unit: find the section that repeats. For addition: open the C=C in the monomer and show –[CH₂–CHR]ₙ–.
Nylon-6,6: two types of monomer (each with 6 carbons). Nylon-6: one monomer (caprolactam, ring-opening). Examiners may ask you to distinguish.
PVC produces toxic HCl when incinerated — this is why disposal is controversial.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation?
flashcards.a: Addition: alkene monomers add across C=C; no small molecule lost. Condensation: difunctional monomers join with loss of H₂O (or HCl) per bond formed.

flashcards.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(propene)?
What bond links monomers in a polyamide?
flashcards.a: Amide bond: –CO–NH– (formed from –COOH and –NH₂ with loss of H₂O).

flashcards.q: Why can polyesters and polyamides be hydrolysed but poly(ethene) cannot?
flashcards.a: Polyesters and polyamides contain hydrolysable ester/amide bonds; poly(ethene) has only C–C and C–H bonds, which are resistant to hydrolysis.

flashcards.q: Why is incineration of PVC controversial?
flashcards.a: PVC contains chlorine; incineration produces toxic HCl gas and potentially dioxins.

questions.q: Which monomer is used to make poly(chloroethene) (PVC)?
questions.exp: PVC is made by addition polymerisation of chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl).

questions.q: What type of bond is the linkage in a polyester?
questions.exp: Polyesters contain –COO– ester linkages formed from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid with loss of H₂O.

questions.q: Which polymer can be hydrolysed by acid or base?
questions.exp: Nylon-6,6 is a polyamide with hydrolysable amide bonds. Addition polymers (poly(ethene) etc.) cannot be hydrolysed.

questions.q: What small molecule is lost in each step of condensation polymerisation between a diol and a diacid?
questions.exp: Each ester bond formed between –OH and –COOH releases one water molecule.

questions.q: HDPE has higher density and hardness than LDPE because:
opts: It is made at higher temperature
Its chains are more linear, allowing closer packing
questions.exp: HDPE has linear chains (Ziegler–Natta catalyst) → closer packing → higher density and stronger intermolecular forces.

recall: Distinguish between addition and condensation polymerisation.
Draw the repeat unit of poly(propene) and poly(chloroethene).
Write the equation for formation of nylon-6,6.
Explain how cross-linking affects polymer properties.
Explain why disposal of addition polymers is an environmental problem.
